name: Wisconsin

agency.name: Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development (DWD), Equal Rights Division, Labor Standards

rates2026.note: Opportunity wage $5.90 for workers under 20 during their first 90 consecutive days

tipped.note: Tips plus wage must average at least $7.25 over the pay period; tipped opportunity employees (under 20, first 90 days) $2.13

minWage.other: Opportunity wage: $5.90 per hour for employees under 20 for their first 90 consecutive calendar days (tipped opportunity employee $2.13). Golf caddies: $5.90 for 9 holes, $10.50 for 18 holes.

source.quote: If you receive tips, your employer must pay you at least $2.33 per hour in wages. If your tips combined with the hourly wage of at least $2.33 per hour do not average at least $7.25 per hour

overtime.note: Time and a half after 40 hours in a workweek; no daily overtime.

source.quote: overtime wages - time and one-half the employee's regular rate of pay - must be paid for all hours worked in excess of 40 in the workweek

sickLeave.note: No state paid sick leave requirement; DWD states employers are not required to provide vacation, holiday or sick pay.

source.quote: Wisconsin employers are not required to provide fringe benefits such as vacation, holiday, or sick pay.

familyLeave.stateUnpaidLaw: Wisconsin Family and Medical Leave Act (unpaid): employers with 50+ permanent employees; employees with 52 consecutive weeks and 1,000 hours. Per year: up to 6 weeks for birth or adoption, 2 weeks to care for a parent, child or spouse, 2 weeks for own serious health condition. Narrower in weeks than the federal FMLA but runs concurrently and covers some different cases (e.g. parents-in-law).

source.quote: An employer must permit the employee to take up to 2 weeks of leave for their own serious health condition in a calendar year, up to 2 weeks for the serious health condition of a parent, child or spouse, and up to 6 weeks for the birth or adoption of a child.

finalPay.fired: on the employer's regular pay schedule (next regular payday)
finalPay.quit: on the employer's regular pay schedule (next regular payday)
finalPay.ptoNote: Depends on the employer's vacation or resignation policy; if there is a written vacation policy without a written forfeiture clause, earned unused vacation must be paid.

source.quote: If you leave employment for any reason, you must be paid in accordance with the employer's regular pay schedule.

ptoSource.quote: Generally, IF the employer implemented a written vacation policy AND it does not include a written forfeit policy, THEN the employer must pay the employee for any earned, unused vacation pay.

breaks.minorsOnly: Under 18: a 30-minute duty-free meal period for every six consecutive hours of work. For adults, DWD only recommends a 30-minute meal break. Breaks under 30 minutes must be paid.

source.quote: If you are 18 years old or older, your employer is not required to give you breaks or meal periods.

notes.text: Short breaks (under 30 consecutive minutes) count as paid work time, and longer breaks must be paid if the employee is not relieved of duties and free to leave.

source.quote: If your authorized break is less than 30 consecutive minutes long, it is counted as work time and must be paid by your employer.

notes.text: Wisconsin's own family leave law lets an employee take up to 2 weeks a year to care for a parent (including a parent-in-law), child or spouse.

source.quote: Under Wisconsin law, an employee is entitled to take up to two weeks per year to care for a parent (including parents-in-law), child, or spouse with a serious health condition.
